_comment: Knowledge base for the traditional chatbot. Each intent has example utterances (used by the TF-IDF matcher), optional regex patterns (checked first), and canned responses (one is chosen at random). Intents with a 'handler' are answered by Python code in skills.py instead of canned text.

responses: Hello! I'm TradBot, a rule-based chatbot. Type 'help' to see what I can do.

examples: what kind of bot are you
responses: I'm TradBot, a traditional (non-LLM) chatbot. I match your message against hand-written rules and a small TF-IDF model, then reply from a fixed knowledge base.
My name is TradBot. I don't use a large language model; I use pattern matching and text similarity to choose answers I was given in advance.

Every message goes through a pipeline: (1) validate and clean the input, (2) try exact regex rules, (3) if none match, compare your words to example phrases using TF-IDF cosine similarity, and (4) if the best score is too low, fall back to a 'did you mean' or 'I don't understand' reply.

examples: what is the chatbot development lifecycle
how do you build a chatbot
responses: A common chatbot development lifecycle is: (1) define the purpose and scope, (2) design conversation flows and intents, (3) collect example utterances and responses, (4) build the NLU and dialogue logic, (5) test with real and malformed inputs, (6) deploy to a channel, and (7) monitor logs and iterate.

examples: what is the difference between a rule based bot and an llm
responses: Traditional bots like me pick from pre-written answers using rules and statistics, so we are predictable, cheap and easy to audit, but we can't answer things we weren't designed for. LLM-based bots generate new text, so they are far more flexible but can be less predictable and need more compute.
